shots.narration_cue: On the afternoon Amy Mihaljevic disappeared, her mother received a phone call from her. An FBI account describes Amy saying she was okay. Her mother believed she was calling from home.
shots.depiction_boundary: No staged caller/child; not a genuine case recording

shots.narration_cue: According to FBI Special Agent Vicki Anderson, Amy was already with the person who had taken her. A familiar kind of check-in had given her mother a mistaken picture of where her daughter was.
shots.depiction_boundary: No staged caller/child; not a genuine case recording

shots.narration_cue: Amy was ten years old and lived in Bay Village, Ohio. She enjoyed riding her bicycle.
shots.depiction_boundary: No stock child presented as Amy; no substitute dog labeled Jake

shots.narration_cue: In a family interview years later, her father, Mark, remembered another part of her life: the horses she rode, and the way she played with their dog, Jake.
shots.depiction_boundary: No stock child presented as Amy; no substitute dog labeled Jake

shots.narration_cue: She had taught him to jump over her legs as though he were a horse. It is a small memory of Amy doing something she loved, before her name became attached to an investigation.
shots.depiction_boundary: No stock child presented as Amy; no substitute dog labeled Jake

shots.narration_cue: Before October 27, 1989, someone had contacted Amy with a plan that involved her mother. The caller said Amy could help choose a gift to celebrate a promotion at work.
shots.depiction_boundary: State the caller’s explanation; do not depict an actual exchange

shots.narration_cue: Bay Village Police place that contact weeks before the disappearance. The meeting was arranged for after school, at a nearby shopping center.
shots.depiction_boundary: State the caller’s explanation; do not depict an actual exchange

shots.narration_cue: The promise of a present for her mother was the reason Amy had been given for going there.
shots.depiction_boundary: State the caller’s explanation; do not depict an actual exchange

shots.narration_cue: That Friday, Amy left school on foot. The FBI says she went to Bay Village Square and was seen outside a business, apparently waiting for someone.
shots.depiction_boundary: No adult/child recreation, vehicle or reconstructed route

shots.narration_cue: The police account describes witnesses seeing her speak with an unidentified man, then walk through the parking lot with him. No vehicle was seen, according to that account.
shots.depiction_boundary: No adult/child recreation, vehicle or reconstructed route

shots.narration_cue: The sighting establishes a public point in the sequence, but it does not reveal where Amy went afterward.
shots.depiction_boundary: No adult/child recreation, vehicle or reconstructed route

shots.narration_cue: Her bicycle was still at school. In a June 2026 interview, her brother, Jason, recalled noticing it there after his own classes ended.
shots.depiction_boundary: Illustrative objects; not Amy’s school/bicycle

shots.narration_cue: News 5's account of the day says their mother later found the bicycle at the school and went to the police to report Amy missing.
shots.depiction_boundary: Illustrative objects; not Amy’s school/bicycle

shots.narration_cue: By then, the expectation that she was safely home had given way to a search for her.

shots.narration_cue: Bay Village Police and the FBI began investigating. Public appeals spread beyond the shopping center.

shots.narration_cue: News 5's reporting describes missing-person posters in shop windows and flyers distributed around the region. A local Pizza Hut put Amy's poster and a composite drawing on its boxes.
shots.depiction_boundary: No invented missing poster or composite; no commercial logo substitute

shots.narration_cue: Those efforts carried the appeal into ordinary places where someone might recognize her or remember the man seen with her.

shots.narration_cue: People were being asked to look back at one afternoon, while investigators had to organize what came in. The public search continued, but Amy did not return home.

shots.narration_cue: On February 8, 1990, a jogger found Amy's body in a field in rural Ashland County. She was wearing the clothing in which she had last been seen.
shots.depiction_boundary: No discovery reenactment, body, road number or asserted crime location

shots.narration_cue: The search for a missing child had become an investigation into her death. The discovery gave investigators another location to examine, beyond the shopping center where she had disappeared.
shots.depiction_boundary: No discovery reenactment, body, road number or asserted crime location

shots.narration_cue: Some of the things believed to have been with her were never recovered. The FBI lists a turquoise horse earring, black ankle boots and a black leather binder. Those objects remain part of its public appeal.
shots.depiction_boundary: No lookalike exhibit or trophy implication

shots.narration_cue: They are details someone might recognize, but the published record does not establish what happened to them. Their absence cannot explain, by itself, who took Amy or where she was killed.
shots.depiction_boundary: No lookalike exhibit or trophy implication

shots.narration_cue: Years later, investigators asked the public to look closely at another object. At a 2016 news conference, authorities displayed a homemade-looking curtain found in the field where Amy's body had been discovered.
shots.depiction_boundary: No generated curtain replica represented as the exhibit

shots.narration_cue: News 5 reported a connection between hair on the curtain and the family's dog. The appeal was for recognition of the textile: where it might have come from, or who might have made it.
shots.depiction_boundary: No generated curtain replica represented as the exhibit

shots.narration_cue: The release brought responses. Cleveland 19 reported that the prosecutor's office received calls and tips afterward, and that law enforcement was following them up.

shots.narration_cue: The curtain offered a possible connection between a physical object and information someone outside the investigation might hold.

shots.narration_cue: Its owner and origin were still questions; the public release did not announce that either had been established.

shots.narration_cue: The investigation also continued through interviews and renewed publicity.

shots.narration_cue: In a report marking thirty years since Amy disappeared, FBI Special Agent Lisa Hack described more than a hundred interviews during her six years working on the case.

shots.narration_cue: She said the files filled seventy volumes. The FBI had also put up billboards around Cleveland and in neighboring states, asking again for information.

shots.narration_cue: Those were accounts of continuing work, not a solved case.
